overview:
Ivory Coast, officially called Côte d'Ivoire, lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, bordered by Liberia, Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Ghana. It is about the size of New Mexico. The official capital is Yamoussoukro, a quiet planned city in the center of the country with one of the largest churches in the world, but the economic heart is Abidjan, a lagoon-side city of skyscrapers and bridges that is one of the biggest French-speaking cities anywhere.

Around 30 million people live in Ivory Coast, including millions of migrants from neighboring countries drawn by its farms and factories. French is the official language, and about 60 local languages, such as Baoulé, Dioula, and Bété, are spoken. The country grows more cocoa than any other nation on Earth, about 40 percent of the world's supply, along with coffee, cashews, and rubber. Ivory Coast is a presidential republic; it was long one of West Africa's most prosperous countries, suffered two civil wars in the 2000s, and has since rebuilt into one of Africa's fastest-growing economies.
landAndNature: The coast is lined with lagoons, sandbars, and beaches, backed by dense rainforest in the south where cocoa and rubber plantations have replaced much of the original forest. Taï National Park protects one of the last big blocks of West African rainforest, home to chimpanzees that crack nuts with stones, pygmy hippos, and forest elephants. The land rises gently to a savanna plateau in the north, and in the west the mountains around Man reach 1,752 meters at Mount Nimba on the Guinean border. Comoé National Park in the northeast is one of the largest protected savannas in West Africa. The Bandama and Sassandra rivers flow south to the sea. Rain is heavy in the south, and the north has a single wet season and a dusty dry season.
peopleAndCulture: The Akan peoples, including the Baoulé, live in the center and east, the Mandé in the northwest, the Gur in the north, and the Kru in the southwest. Islam and Christianity are both widespread. Attiéké, a couscous-like dish of grated cassava, is eaten with grilled fish and spicy sauce, and kedjenou is chicken slow-cooked in a sealed pot. Ivory Coast is the birthplace of coupé-décalé and zouglou dance music, and the reggae star Alpha Blondy came from here. Dance masks of the Baoulé, Dan, and Senufo peoples are prized by museums worldwide. Soccer is the great passion: the national team, the Elephants, won the Africa Cup of Nations three times, including as hosts in 2024, and produced stars such as Didier Drogba.
history: Kingdoms such as Kong and the Baoulé state of Queen Pokou flourished before Europeans arrived; the coast got its name from the ivory that traders sought in the 1400s and 1500s. France established control in the late 1800s and made Ivory Coast a colony in 1893, building plantations and the port of Abidjan. Félix Houphouët-Boigny led the country to independence on August 7, 1960 and ruled for 33 years, keeping close ties with France and turning cocoa and coffee into an economic miracle. After his death in 1993, disputes over who counted as truly Ivorian led to a coup in 1999 and civil wars in 2002 and 2010 to 2011, the latter after a disputed election. Peace returned, and Abidjan has boomed with new bridges, highways, and towers.
funFacts: Ivory Coast produces about 40 percent of the world's cocoa, so roughly two of every five chocolate bars start here.
The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is one of the largest churches on Earth, modeled on St. Peter's in Rome.
The country asked in 1986 that all languages call it Côte d'Ivoire, its French name, instead of translations.
Ivory Coast hosted and won the 2024 Africa Cup of Nations after nearly being eliminated in the group stage.
Pygmy hippos, which weigh about a tenth as much as regular hippos, live in the forests of Taï National Park.
